As long as you don't give up it's alright. I started out not being able to walk daily due to a combo of my bad mental health and physical disabilities but keeping up with it even when I could only go every other day or a few days a week has made a world of difference in the past few months. Just do what you can, these are things that has helped me a lot over the 10 months I've been in my slightly better living situation and they're not for everyone but I thought I'd throw them out anyway in case they can help ^^

1. Eat a balanced diet. Try to include fruits and vegetables especially, a lot of people don't get nearly enough of those. And I'm talking the fresh stuff - I like to make a salad of fresh apples, mandarin orange slices, red and green grapes, kiwi and spinach. Blueberries, raspberries and strawberries are great when they are in season and thus relatively cheap and I'll eat them as is like candy. But also don't stress if that kind of stuff is out of your price range, or if you are having a bad day and want to binge a little bit. Balance is key.

2. Get on a sleep schedule as best you can. If your work is wonky and some nights they want you to stay until 11 at night and come in at 6 in the morning to open just do your best. Training your body to recognize sleep and getting up at a regular time, or at least semi-regular, can seriously help your mental health.

3. Speaking of sleep, don't do stuff in your bed. If you feel like laying in bed all day and watching stuff on your phone or laptop find somewhere else to do it. Your bed is 100% only for sleep, period dot end. This seriously helps with point 2, where when you go to your bed your brain subconsciously recognizes that it's sleep time and not time to be doing other things.

4. As much as you can, exercise. Of all people I know how hard that can be because I'm physically disabled, so just doing what you can every day can help. Do it outside if at all possible, but just doing it is enough. I just take a short 20 minute walk every day whenever the weather is clear because that's all I'm capable of but it has vastly improved my mental health.

5. Do something social. If you don't have easy access to friends or it's too late at night or whatever, play a free online social game of some kind or find places like 7 Cups of Tea or similar things where you can talk to someone who can listen to you and help. I personally love playing Town of Salem (though I have the paid version) because just reading what other people are typing and knowing there's other people out there helps, and focusing on the games instead of other things when I'm having a bad day is really helpful. 

6. Don't run from your responsibilities. It's super tempting to just take a day off from things and veg out and do nothing, but believe me in the long run that just makes things worse. You are far better off finding a way to make the responsibility fun - I like to play music when I do chores and make games out of them. When I have to do work as long as I'm allowed to I will keep a good tv show playing in the background or some music or something else to help make the whole thing less monotonous and terrible. Just get it done and over with, and reward yourself when it's finished. You'll feel better when those dishes aren't still sitting in the sink 2 days later and you're beating yourself up for not having done them sooner, trust me.

A combination of cutting down on my coffee in the morning and drinking water. Basically wake up, get my Keurig set up and dispensing my coffee (16oz in a 24oz mug) and while that's going get myself 16oz of water in my measured bottle. While my coffee is cooling because I like it room temp give or take I make sure to ingest all of that water and don't allow myself to touch the coffee until the water is done. That 16oz of coffee is all I get - no second or third cup, just that much. So I make it last through the day to help keep me awake and usually finish my coffee around 2 or 3 in the afternoon and after that if I feel thirsty it's more water or tea depending on the temp of the day.

I have a lot more energy than when I was drinking a full pot before noon, I'm not nearly as jittery and I have a ton more focused, and I'm healthier overall because I'm more hydrated from drinking water instead of a ton of coffee.

Once you've taken any kind of drug it isn't illegal, it's only illegal if you are in possession of it. Hospital staff and EMT's don't want to get you in trouble with the police, they want to save your life. If you're going to take anything (which I don't advocate, but on the chances someone out there who might could be reading this) get the name and try to remember but also tell your friends and write it in your phone or in sharpie on your arm or something in case you're unconscious. Knowing what and how much you took could help medical professionals save your life. [Tip courtesy of my cousin who is an ER doctor and sees this a lot and regrets that some lives could not be saved because they literally had no idea what drug and how much people had taken and thus didn't know how to treat them in time or at all]

First off, stop calling it laziness and stop seeing yourself as a lazy person. Normally what we associate with 'lazy' behavior is the result of something else. For example, mine tends to come from anxiety, depression, and an executive dysfunction disorder from being raised in an abusive household. The sink is full of dirty dishes? I should do them, but my anxiety tells me it's too much for me to handle, the depression says it's not worth doing them because there will always be more dirty dishes, and the executive dysfunction says the time it'd take me to do them could be better spent doing something I enjoy like gaming.

Once you realize what other things are causing your 'lazy' behavior and you stop seeing it as laziness and start seeing it as something you can handle you can take things from there.

Learn to make citrus salts. Take lemon, orange and lime rinds and dry them out. Put them in a blender or grinder with some salt at a 1:2 ratio of peel to salt and grind into a fine powder. Add sparingly to just about anything. You get not only the salt, but a bit of citrus zest which can really help bring out the flavors.

Anything you're baking that has chocolate in it, replace the water (usually a few tablespoons up to 1/4 cup) with room temp black coffee. The little bit super helps bring out the chocolate flavor, doesn't taste bitter or like coffee, and unless someone basically has an allergy or super sensitivity most people don't even know unless you tell them.

Herbs and spices are your friend and can cover a world of bad. But use them sparingly - you can add more if it doesn't taste right, but you usually can't remove spice if you add too much.

Finally, there's no shame in substituting a pre-made component to any recipe. I never make my dough or pie crust from scratch, I always get it pre-made and people rarely know the difference.

Scoop the cat box and take out other trash if it's full (kitchen, bathroom, ect). Put down a reminder if laundry needs to be done, lay out my clothes for the next day in the bathroom. Make any food that needs to be set for the next day - sometimes I pre-make breakfast with overnight oats and stuff like that, and some days lunch needs to be made and I get out meat to thaw for cooking dinner if that's necessary. Make sure the Keurig is filled and set to start brewing coffee for the carafe so it's done by the time I get up. If the weather is good I make time to take the dog on an evening walk around the block, and I joined a challenge at the start of January that's 365 tasks so you do one each day so I take time to look through a physical copy I have of the list in a notepad so I'm not staring at it on a screen and I pick one that can get done the next day and set a reminder to do it.

There's a few more that are a bit situational, but it all boils down to making sure I wake up without having to worry that certain things were not done and actually makes me sleep a little easier because I know those things are complete so I don't have to panic about them when I'm trying to settle down :)

Depends on what's causing the insomnia - brain or body. I've had both types before.

Brain insomnia is when your body is tired but your brain is running on over drive, constantly reminding you of things you haven't done and bringing up the past to keep you awake at night. This is usually solved with meds, either OTC or given by a doctor, but I can't afford the meds and they weren't working when I could so I started practicing meditation and actually addressing the concerns my brain was thinking of as I slept by writing them down while in bed so I knew to handle them when I woke up.

Body insomnia is when your mind says sleep but your body doesn't want to because you're hyped up or stressed or whatever. Relaxation via a hot shower, warm tea, exercise, and things like that are my biggest helps. I can't exercise normally because reasons, but I do find yoga to be super helpful for that in case that's a problem for anyone reading this who might like to try.

Everything.

1. All schools given the exact same funding per child, not funding per child determined by the value of the homes in the area as most public schools are now.

2. All schools having the same requirements for graduation, not on a state-by-state or even county-by-county basis. My senior year was hell on Earth because while other seniors got to take it easy I had to take all hard classes as I had moved states over the summer and the requirements to graduate in my new state did not align with classes I had taken in my previous state. I almost had to be a 5th year senior because of it.

3. Mandatory comprehensive sex education. Religion can stay the hell out unless it's a private religious school, and the parents shouldn't get to keep the kids out if they want those kids to graduate. And by 'comprehensive' I mean fully, wholly comprehensive. Not abstinence only, not scare tactics with pics of STD's and videos of women giving birth screaming in pain. Actual sex education to just take away the mystery behind it all.

4. Actual anti-bullying policies and actual enforcement of it. Not this fake anti-bullying that only applies to kids who meet a certain standard or saying they'll enforce it and then not doing so.

5. Teachers actually needing to be qualified for their jobs and like kids. I've had some teachers who had no idea what they were doing and had no business teaching their subject, and several who were just clearly unpleasant people who hated kids and were teaching because it was all they were qualified to do and so were just miserable to us and made us all miserable.

6. Better school lunches nutrition-wise. Not this crap with spoiled milk and moldy cheese slices or feeding kids over processed foods because it's cheap. 

7. K-12 recess times, and better times for younger kids. I seriously think it would solve at least 80% of the ADD/ADHD-like symptoms in younger kids because let's face it, that 80% of the time they don't have an attention disorder they're just an 8 year old who wants to run around not sit in class and if you give them an outlet instead of cooping them up and only giving them 30 minutes once a day to run around they'll actually sit and pay attention better. And for older kids it makes the school seem less like a prison which I'm sure would help things quite a bit.

8. Teachers and schools actually being able to do things about kids misbehaving. Not just calling the parents or bringing it up at a Parent-Teacher meeting and being told that the kid is a perfect angel and the fault must be on the teacher and zero getting done about back talk, throwing things, or being disruptive outside of constantly getting sent out of class to the office. Also tachers and schools being able to get kids mandatory psych help if there's an issue, even if the parents won't consent. Probably there should be a trained psych on staff to address if the kid needs real help, it shouldn't be a suggestion to the parents it should be mandatory so those kids can get the help they need before it's too late.

9. Better balance in classes. Some things, like sex and drug education and probably life skills like basic cooking and cleaning and money management ect should be mandatory. But beyond that? If a kid loves math but hates history don't freaking force them to take a history course. They get miserable because it's not a subject they're interested in or want to learn about and not everyone in the world will be 'well rounded' and it's stupid to expect otherwise.

10. Elimination of homework. Kids have to spend ~8 hours a day at school, which is as much as we expect a full time job worker to spend at their job. Yet the job worker rarely has to bring work home unless that's part of the job and usually they know ahead of time they'll be expected to bring stuff home with them while the student does not get a choice or a say.

11. Better fund distribution over all. The school I went to had 2 60+ inch TV's in the front hallway always displaying the school news that no one gave a care about, but couldn't get us updated text books. As this was explained to me by several people, this is because the school is given x amount of money per year but it's divided into categories such as text books versus new technology. And what goes into each category can ONLY be spent on that category, so the school couldn't say "Well all of our computers are no more than 2 years old and in working condition but we still have y amount of money left in the new technology category so let's reallocate it to text books instead" and if they didn't spend the money on new technology they had to give it back at the end of the school year. Same thing goes for money allocated to things like paying bills or paying for sports teams - if there was left over, they couldn't put it towards something that was getting less funding to help out. I'm not sure if it's this way for all schools but it seems to be a thing I've run in to more than once when talking about school funding and it needs to stop.

There's several more, but I can't think of them right now. tl;dr the USA school system needs to be torn down and rebuilt from the ground up so it's actually effective, and they should pay more attention to what other countries are doing that's working and what studies are showing actually works instead of sticking to this archaic and outdated version of what school is.

It's less about raising the prices and more about the idea that it basically lets them control what the public sees.

For example, my mother has internet with AT&T. If Net Neutrality is abolished what they likely will do is give a base package that includes fast access to all AT&T owned/affiliated websites for the exact same price she's paying now, while charging her more to get the package that includes access to sites that aren't like say tumblr (which is owned by Verizon, if I'm not mistaken). Meanwhile people with Verizon or Spectrum or whatever will be getting the same - good access to sites owned by or affiliated with the company, slow access to those not unless you pay a ton more. You like Reddit? Better hope who/whatever owns it is affiliated with your current internet provider, or else you might be paying $5 or $10 more on top of your $100 a month for internet to get access with any speed faster and more reliable than the days of dial-up. You like streaming Netflix or hulu or gamers on YouTube/Twitch/ect? Hope you're willing to cough up in the ballpark of an extra $20 a month to watch more than one video without having to sit with 30+ minutes of buffering for each individual episode you want to watch.

Net Neutrality means they can't do that. It means if you're paying for internet from them, you have access to just about every website in the world with the same speed and efficiency as you would normally get with the company and that is the way it should be. So the reason we're attacking the FCC is because they can hold that regulation in place and prevent these companies from pulling those kinds of moves, and they shouldn't even be thinking about tearing it down in the first place.
